extracted.intended_audience: authors of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Cochrane review authors, evidence synthesis researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for summarising study characteristics, deciding which studies to group for each planned comparison, determining available data for synthesis, handling multiplicity, and preparing for statistical or other synthesis methods in systematic reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of PICO to use in synthesis planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish three types of PICO: the review PICO (planned at protocol stage; eligibility), the PICO for each synthesis (defines the question each synthesis aims to answer and planned comparisons), and the PICO of the included studies (what was actually investigated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the PICO for each synthesis and the PICO of included studies as the basis for determining which studies can be grouped for statistical synthesis and for synthesizing study characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan comparisons at protocol stage (Step 1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: At protocol stage set up the comparisons and specify which characteristics of interventions, populations, outcomes and study design will be grouped together for synthesis (the PICO for each synthesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planning for the synthesis should start at protocol-writing stage to pre-specify grouping rules and reduce post-hoc decisions (see Chapter 2 and Chapter 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize characteristics of each study (Step 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the PICO characteristics of each study in a ‘Characteristics of included studies’ table, categorizing PICO elements into the pre-specified groups in the protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize descriptions (apply labels/terminology from the PICO for each synthesis), structure descriptions, and include key intervention characteristics (e.g. duration, frequency) to facilitate comparison. Use structured tables rather than long text when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize labels and terminology across studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where study terminology varies, apply the labels and terminology used to articulate the PICO for each synthesis and structure descriptions to facilitate comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization includes coding intervention components into pre-specified categories and coding variables such as duration and frequency into standard categories to enable meta-regression and transparent grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TIDieR to structure intervention descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe interventions using a structured template such as the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) to capture content and characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TIDieR (and similar checklists) helps itemize intervention content and other characteristics needed to decide which studies can be grouped for synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize interventions into pre-specified groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign the main intervention strategy of each study to one of the pre-defined groups (e.g. counselling, incentives, social support) as specified in the PICO for each synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide definitions for each group (eligible modes of delivery, duration, personnel) and code additional components (e.g. booster sessions) to determine eligibility for comparisons (example: Table 9.3.a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine which studies are similar enough to group (Step 2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the coded PICO elements across studies to decide which studies can be grouped within each comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate characteristics (by comparison or by PICO elements) to explore similarity; choose level of detail appropriate to the review's purpose. Use matrices or structured summary tables to identify potentially important differences pre-specified as effect modifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabulate study characteristics to enable comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Create tables that summarize intervention/comparator groups, important components, outcomes measured and time points to show similarity across studies contributing to a synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering (e.g. by comparator) and grouping outcomes into pre-specified domains/time frames makes it easier to see the number of studies contributing to a particular synthesis and to plan alternative methods if meta-analysis is not possible (see Table 9.3.b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess appropriateness of measurement tools for outcome domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must assess whether the measurement methods/tools used within each study provide an appropriate assessment of the pre-specified outcome domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assessment informs grouping of measures into outcome domains and selection of which measure to include in a synthesis (see Chapter 3, Section 3.2.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and group time frames (short-term, long-term, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group outcome measures into pre-specified time points (e.g. short-term and long-term) according to definitions chosen in the PICO for each synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: short-term <6 weeks; long-term ≥6 weeks to 12 months. When multiple time points fall within a time frame specify rules (e.g. choose the longest time point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what data are available for synthesis (Step 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the extracted statistics, measurement instruments and time frames to assess what effect estimates and variance measures are available for inclusion in synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate available statistics (e.g. mean, SD, SE, median, IQR) and mark whether a study contributes required data for meta-analysis. Reordering tables by comparison/outcome/time frame shows how many studies will contribute to a given meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and handle multiplicity of outcomes/measures/time points
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplicity arises from multiple instruments measuring the same domain or multiple time points within the same time frame; pre-specified methods should be used to select which effect estimate to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of approaches (Table 9.3.c): random selection; averaging of effect estimates (with variance calculation); median effect estimate; decision rules (hierarchies based on clinical or methodological relevance). Specify hierarchy/order if multiple rules applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select outcome using pre-specified decision rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use decision rules to choose the most relevant outcome when multiple are available within an outcome domain, based on clinical or methodological considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision rules can be hierarchical (e.g. prefer global pain, then pain on walking, then WOMAC pain subscore, etc.). If multiple time points exist within a time frame, select according to pre-specified preference (e.g. longest time point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify planned comparisons/outcomes only with rationale (Step 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If preliminary examination reveals important variations or sparse data, planned comparisons or outcome groupings may need modification; authors should report rationale for any post-hoc changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planning contingencies in the protocol reduces post-hoc decision making. If changes are made (e.g. splitting shape vs size into separate comparisons), provide rationale and note that it was post-hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize characteristics of studies contributing to each comparison (Step 2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate information about key PICO characteristics across studies contributing to a comparison, identifying potentially important differences pre-specified as effect modifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesis of study characteristics is essential for interpreting combined effects and for GRADE assessments (indirectness and inconsistency). Use tables to present information concisely and transparently, and ensure studies not contributing to combined effects are accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check data accuracy before synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare magnitudes and directions of effects reported by studies with how they will be presented in the review to identify typographical errors, extraction/entry errors, or other inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure qualitative findings (direction, statistical significance) are consistent between source reports and review. Forest plot results should agree with original reports if same effect measure/statistical model used. Legitimate reasons for differences include different effect measures, choice of change-from-baseline vs post-only, grouping similar interventions, or unit-of-analysis adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabulate extracted data including available statistics and effect SEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Record available data (e.g. mean, SD, N; median, IQR; MD and 95% CI; MD and SE) in tables that indicate whether effect estimate and standard error can be computed for meta-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a 'Data' column and an 'Effect & SE' column (or similar) to show which studies contribute computable data. Note when imputation, conversion, or author contact may be needed to obtain required statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imputation/conversion/contact authors when data incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: Where studies lack required statistics, compute estimates via imputation, convert between statistics (e.g. medians to means), or contact study authors to obtain missing data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag studies where imputation or conversion has been used; indicate uncertainty. Such methods may allow additional studies to contribute to meta-analysis (see notes in Table 9.3.b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan contingencies to use alternative synthesis methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Build contingencies into the analysis plan to use alternative summary/synthesis methods if the desired method (e.g. meta-analysis) is not possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider narrative summaries, vote counting, combining P values, summary of effect estimates, or other methods (Chapter 12) when meta-analysis cannot be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate synthesis method for the question
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the synthesis method that addresses the review question and matches the available data: text/tabular summary, vote counting, combining P values, summary of effect estimates, pairwise meta-analysis, network meta-analysis, subgroup analysis/meta-regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 9.5.a maps methods to questions they address (e.g. 'Is there any evidence of an effect?' vs 'What is the average intervention effect?') and gives example plots associated with methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate visual displays for synthesis and exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ suitable plots to present individual study effects, distributions, directions, and network relationships (e.g. forest plots, harvest plots, effect direction plots, albatross plots, box-and-whisker plots, bubble plots, network diagrams, rankograms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose visuals that support the synthesis method (e.g. forest plots for meta-analysis, network diagrams for network meta-analysis) and help readers inspect consistency and heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and report deviations and rationale transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Any deviations from pre-specified plans (groupings, outcomes, or analytical choices) should be described and justified in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent reporting of post-hoc decisions helps readers assess the potential for bias introduced by analysis choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer tabulation over lengthy textual description for transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabulating study characteristics and extracted data is generally preferable to lengthy narrative description for enabling rapid scanning and identification of patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables can improve transparency of grouping decisions and help reviewers and readers see which studies contribute to combined effects and which do not.
